questions.title: Cell death as a sign of irreversible cell injury
questions.question: Cell death is a sign of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. "General response to cellular stress" is too broad and does not specify an outcome; a cell under stress may adapt, be reversibly injured, or die, and this option names none of those three specific endpoints.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Reversible cell injury is, by definition, an injury that resolves and returns the cell to normal if the stimulus is removed -- it does not end in cell death, which is the opposite endpoint.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cellular adaptation is the response to modest, sustained stress that preserves cell viability (e.g. hypertrophy, atrophy, metaplasia) -- it is not a form of cell death.
explanations.D: Correct. A cell meets stress with adaptation, reversible injury, or irreversible injury and death, forming one continuum of progressively worse impairment. Cell death itself only occurs once injury has crossed into the irreversible portion of that continuum -- by definition, a cell that dies has sustained damage beyond the point of recovery, which is exactly what "irreversible" means in this framework.

questions.learning_objective: Place cell death on the adaptation-reversible-irreversible continuum as the outcome of irreversible injury specifically.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Irreversible cell injury"

questions.title: Necrosis as an example of irreversible cell injury
questions.question: Irreversible cell injury includes:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hydropic swelling (cell swelling from sodium and water accumulation) is a classic example of reversible cell injury -- it resolves if the stimulus is removed, which is the opposite of irreversible.
explanations.B: Correct. Necrosis is the pathological process by which cells die following irreversible injury. It is the standard worked example of an irreversible outcome on the cell-stress continuum. Unlike adaptation or reversible injury, once necrosis has occurred the cell cannot be restored to normal, however promptly the injurious stimulus is removed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Fatty change (steatosis, lipid accumulation within a cell) is a reversible cellular accumulation, not a form of cell death, and resolves once the causative stimulus is removed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cloudy swelling is a mild, reversible cellular accumulation (an early, low-grade form of cell swelling), not an example of irreversible injury.

questions.learning_objective: Identify necrosis as the worked example of irreversible cell injury, and distinguish it from the reversible cellular-accumulation examples (hydropic swelling, fatty change, cloudy swelling).

questions.title: Mechanisms by which stimuli cause cellular injury
questions.question: Stimuli causing cellular injury do so by:

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own. Increased free-radical production is a real mechanism of cell injury (it damages membranes, proteins and DNA), but it is not the only mechanism, and this quiz's own printed key marks all three named mechanisms together as correct, not this one alone.
explanations.B: Correct. Cell injury proceeds through several linked mechanisms together, not any single one alone: interference with mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation depletes ATP, which disables the energy-dependent pump that normally keeps intracellular calcium low, so calcium rises; free radicals, generated by the same injurious stimuli (ischaemia-reperfusion, toxins, radiation), independently damage membranes, proteins and DNA. All three -- ATP depletion, calcium rise, and free-radical accumulation -- are genuine, simultaneously-acting mechanisms of cell injury, which is why the printed key marks all of the individually-listed options as correct together.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own. ATP depletion is a real mechanism of cell injury (it disables the sodium pump and the calcium-clearing pump), but it is not the only mechanism, and this quiz's own printed key marks all three named mechanisms together as correct, not this one alone.
explanations.D: Incorrect on its own. Increased intracellular calcium is a real and centrally important mechanism of cell injury, activating phospholipases, proteases and endonucleases, but it is not the only mechanism, and this quiz's own printed key marks all three named mechanisms together as correct, not this one alone.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that free-radical production, ATP depletion and calcium rise act together, not as mutually exclusive alternative mechanisms of cell injury.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: All are correct"

questions.title: A defining character of atrophy
questions.question: Which of the following is a character of atrophy?

options.A: Increase in size and number of cells
options.C: May result from a disuse of organ

explanations.A: Incorrect. Atrophy is a decrease, not an increase, in cell size and number -- this option describes the opposite direction of change from what defines atrophy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Being precancerous describes dysplasia, not atrophy -- atrophy is a benign shrinkage of tissue, not a step toward malignancy.
explanations.C: Correct. Atrophy is the adaptive shrinkage of a cell or organ that follows reduced functional demand, and disuse (reduced workload on a muscle, for example) is one of its classic causes, alongside reduced blood supply, reduced nutrition, reduced hormonal or nervous stimulation, and ageing. A disused limb muscle immobilised in a cast is the textbook worked example of disuse atrophy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Congenital" describes a condition present from birth, which is not how atrophy is characterised -- atrophy is an acquired shrinkage of a previously normal-sized, previously formed tissue, not a developmental anomaly present at birth.

questions.learning_objective: State disuse as a cause of atrophy, and distinguish atrophy from precancerous change and from a congenital condition.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: May result from a disuse of organ"

questions.title: What atrophy is not
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT true as regard atrophy?

explanations.A: This IS true of atrophy, so it is not the answer being asked for. Skeletal muscle is a common and classic site of atrophy, particularly disuse atrophy of an immobilised limb.
explanations.B: This IS true of atrophy, so it is not the answer being asked for. Disuse (reduced functional demand on a tissue) is one of atrophy's standard causes.
explanations.C: Correct -- this is the false statement. Atrophy is defined as a decrease, not an increase, in cell size and/or number. "Increase in cell number" instead describes hyperplasia, the opposite adaptive response, so this statement does not hold for atrophy.
explanations.D: This IS true of atrophy, so it is not the answer being asked for. Ageing is a recognised, common cause of atrophy (senile atrophy) in multiple organs, alongside disuse, reduced blood supply and reduced hormonal or nervous stimulation.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that atrophy is defined by decreased, not increased, cell number, distinguishing it from hyperplasia.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Defined as increase cell number"

questions.title: Definition of metaplasia
questions.question: Change of one type of tissue into another type is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neoplasia is new, uncontrolled and excessive growth of cells, benign or malignant -- it does not describe one differentiated tissue type converting into another.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hypoplasia is underdevelopment of an organ (fewer cells than normal formed during development), not a conversion of one tissue type into another.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dysplasia is disordered growth with loss of uniformity of individual cells and their architectural orientation -- an abnormal pattern within the same tissue type, not a change from one tissue type into another.
explanations.D: Correct. Metaplasia is the reversible replacement of one differentiated adult cell type by another, better able to withstand the new stress. The standard worked example is the columnar respiratory epithelium of a smoker's bronchus converting to stratified squamous epithelium -- a change of one tissue type into another type in response to a sustained irritant.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells of the same type, not a change of one tissue type into a different one.

questions.learning_objective: Define metaplasia as the reversible conversion of one differentiated tissue type into another, distinct from neoplasia, hypoplasia, dysplasia and hyperplasia.

questions.title: A defining character of hyperplasia
questions.question: Which of the following is true as regard hyperplasia?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Disuse causes atrophy (shrinkage from reduced demand), which is the opposite adaptive response to hyperplasia -- hyperplasia instead typically follows increased functional demand or hormonal stimulation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Skeletal muscle cells are terminally differentiated and cannot ordinarily divide, so true hyperplasia (an increase in cell number by mitosis) is not a feature of skeletal muscle -- an enlarging skeletal muscle instead grows chiefly by hypertrophy of existing fibres.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Old age is more classically associated with atrophy (senile atrophy) than with hyperplasia, which is instead a response to increased demand or stimulation, not a general feature of ageing tissue.
explanations.D: Correct. Hyperplasia is defined as an increase in the number of cells in an organ or tissue, achieved by mitotic division of cells that retain the capacity to proliferate. It is the direct counterpart to atrophy, which is instead defined by decreased cell number and size, so the two sit at opposite ends of the same size-of-organ spectrum.

questions.learning_objective: Define hyperplasia as an increase in cell number, and recognise that it does not apply to terminally differentiated tissue such as skeletal muscle.
